books.title: Why We Sleep
books.author: Matthew Walker
books.description: A sleep scientist explains what sleep does for the brain and body, and what happens when we skimp on it.
ideas: Sleep is a performance tool

Sleep isn't the absence of activity; it's one of the busiest things your brain does. Matthew Walker, a sleep scientist, describes how the sleeping brain sorts memories, clears out waste and resets emotional balance. Regularly sleeping six hours or less impairs focus, mood and immunity, often without people noticing how much they've slipped. Many of us treat sleep as optional, the first thing we cut when life gets busy. Walker argues it's the foundation everything else rests on. Today: pick a consistent wake-up time and stick to it, even at weekends. It's one of the simplest ways to steady your sleep.
sleep-performance
Sleep before and after learning

Sleep before learning prepares the brain to soak up new information, like clearing a desk before work. Sleep after learning helps lock those memories in, moving them into long-term storage. Walker points out that pulling an all-nighter before an exam undermines both: you learn less and remember less of what you did learn. Students who sleep well often outperform those who cram. Today: if you're learning something new, a language, an instrument or a work skill, practise in the evening and let a full night's sleep finish the job.
Caffeine lingers

Caffeine blocks a sleep-pressure chemical in the brain called adenosine, which is why coffee wakes you up. But it lingers: its half-life is around five to six hours, so half of an afternoon coffee may still be active at bedtime. Many people fall asleep anyway but get lighter, less refreshing sleep without realising why. Walker recommends being careful with caffeine after midday. Today: try moving your last coffee or tea to before lunch for a week and notice whether your sleep feels deeper.
Keep the bedroom cool and dark

To fall asleep, your body needs to drop its core temperature by a degree or two. That's why it's harder to sleep in a stuffy room and why a warm bath before bed, which pulls heat to the skin, can help. Light matters too: bright screens in the evening tell the brain it's still daytime and delay the sleep hormone melatonin. A cool, dark, quiet bedroom is one of the cheapest health upgrades there is. Today: dim the lights an hour before bed, open a window or turn the heating down, and see how quickly you drift off.
Dreams as overnight therapy

During REM sleep, the dreaming phase, the brain revisits emotional memories in a calmer chemical state, with stress chemicals turned down. Walker describes this as a kind of overnight therapy: it softens the emotional sting of difficult experiences while preserving their lessons. That's part of why problems often feel smaller in the morning and why poor sleep makes us more reactive. Today: if you're upset about something, resist the urge to settle it late at night. Sleep on it, and look at it again with a rested mind.

books.title: Give Your Ideas Some Legs
books.author: Oppezzo & Schwartz
books.description: Stanford experiments on how walking affects creative thinking.
ideas: Walk to think better

Stuck on a problem? Go for a walk. In experiments at Stanford University, people came up with significantly more creative ideas while walking than while sitting, for example when asked to think of unusual uses for everyday objects. The boost even lingered for a short while after they sat back down. Philosophers like Nietzsche and writers like Dickens were famous walkers, and now there's data to support their habit. Movement seems to loosen the mind. Today: the next time you're stuck on a decision or a piece of writing, take a ten-minute walk and let your thoughts wander.
walk-to-think
Indoors works too

You might assume the creative boost from walking comes from fresh air and scenery. Surprisingly, it showed up even when participants walked on a treadmill facing a blank wall. The act of walking itself seemed to free up ideas. That's good news for anyone in a city, on a rainy day or stuck in an office: pacing a corridor or a lap of the building can be enough. Today: if you can't get outside, walk around your home or office for five minutes while thinking about a problem, and jot down whatever comes to mind.
Walking meetings

Sitting across a table can make conversations feel formal or confrontational. Walking side by side often makes them easier: people talk more freely, ideas flow and silences feel less awkward. Some leaders hold walking meetings for brainstorming or difficult discussions. You get exercise, fresh perspectives and better ideas at the same time. It works for personal conversations too, like talking with a teenager or a struggling friend. Today: suggest a walking chat instead of a sit-down meeting for your next one-on-one conversation.

books.title: Outlive
books.author: Peter Attia
books.description: A physician's approach to extending not just lifespan but healthspan: the years you live in good health.
ideas: Healthspan over lifespan

Living longer is only half the goal. Peter Attia, a physician focused on longevity, emphasises healthspan: the years you spend in good physical and mental health. Many people live into their eighties but spend the last decade struggling with frailty, pain or memory loss. The aim is to stay strong, sharp and capable as long as possible, so that the extra years are worth living. Today: picture yourself at eighty-five. What do you want to still be able to do, carry groceries, travel, play with grandchildren? Let that picture guide your choices this week.
Exercise is the strongest medicine

If a pill did what exercise does for health, Attia suggests, it would be the most prescribed medicine in the world. Cardiorespiratory fitness and muscle strength are among the strongest predictors of how long and how well people live, more than many risk factors we worry about. Being in the bottom fitness group carries more risk than smoking in some studies. The good news is that improving from very unfit to moderately fit brings big benefits. Today: schedule two sessions of exercise into your week, and treat them like appointments with a doctor.
Train for your centenarian decathlon

Attia suggests a vivid exercise called the centenarian decathlon. Make a list of physical tasks you want to be able to do at ninety or a hundred: get up off the floor without help, lift a suitcase into an overhead bin, carry a grandchild, climb a flight of stairs. Then work backwards. Since strength and fitness decline with age, you need to build a big reserve now to have enough left later. Today: write your own list of five things you want to do at ninety, and choose one exercise that trains for it.
Zone 2 cardio

Zone 2 cardio is steady exercise at an effort where you can still talk in full sentences but would rather not, like brisk walking, gentle cycling or easy jogging. Attia believes it's one of the best ways to build the aerobic base and metabolic health that protect against disease. It's not glamorous, and it doesn't leave you gasping, but a few hours a week pay off over decades. Today: go for a thirty-minute walk or ride at a pace where conversation is possible but a little effortful. That's zone 2.
Prevention starts early

Heart disease, type 2 diabetes and dementia don't appear overnight. They develop silently over decades. Attia argues that waiting until symptoms show up is like trying to fix a leaking roof during the storm. The time to act is in your thirties and forties, or now, whatever your age, through exercise, sleep, nutrition and regular check-ups. Prevention is far more powerful than treatment. Today: if you haven't had a recent health check, book one, and ask about blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol.

books.title: In Defense of Food
books.author: Michael Pollan
books.description: A clear argument for simple eating rules in a world of confusing nutrition advice.
ideas: Eat food. Not too much. Mostly plants.

Michael Pollan sums up his whole approach to eating in seven words: eat food, not too much, mostly plants. "Food" means real food rather than highly processed products; "not too much" means paying attention to portions; "mostly plants" means vegetables, fruits, beans and whole grains making up most of your plate. It's not a diet so much as a return to common sense, and it frees you from the confusing swings of nutrition headlines. Today: at your next meal, fill half your plate with vegetables or fruit before adding anything else.
Beware of health claims

It's a strange pattern: foods that loudly announce their health benefits are usually processed. Breakfast cereals claim to boost immunity; snack bars promise protein and fibre. Meanwhile, broccoli and apples don't need labels at all. Pollan suggests being wary of health claims on packaging; they're often marketing that distracts from sugar, additives or heavy processing. Today: when shopping, notice which items have health claims on the front, and compare their ingredient lists with simple, unpackaged foods.
Your great-grandmother test

Pollan offers a simple test: don't eat anything your great-grandmother wouldn't recognise as food. She'd know an egg, a carrot or a loaf of bread, but she'd be baffled by a tube of brightly coloured yogurt with a long list of unpronounceable ingredients. Another rule: avoid products with more than five ingredients, or ingredients you can't picture. These rules aren't perfect, but they quickly steer you toward real food. Today: pick one processed item you eat often, read its label, and look for a simpler alternative.
Shop the edges

In many supermarkets, the fresh food, produce, meat, fish, dairy and bread, sits around the outer walls, while processed foods fill the middle aisles. Pollan suggests shopping mostly along the edges. It's not a perfect rule, since there are good things in the middle like beans, oats and frozen vegetables, but it's a useful habit for filling your basket with whole foods. Today: on your next shopping trip, start with the outer aisles and see how much of your list you can complete before going into the centre.
Eat slowly, at a table

Pollan observes that how we eat matters as much as what we eat. Eating at regular meals, at a table, with other people and without screens tends to slow us down. We notice when we're full, enjoy flavours more and eat less mindlessly. Many cultures with strong food traditions eat this way and stay healthier despite rich foods. Today: eat one meal sitting at a table with no phone or TV, chew slowly, and put your fork down between bites.

books.title: Breath
books.author: James Nestor
books.description: A journalist explores how the way we breathe affects health, sleep and performance.
ideas: Breathe through your nose

Your nose isn't just for smelling. It filters, warms and humidifies the air you breathe, and it helps your body absorb oxygen efficiently. James Nestor, who experimented with breathing only through his mouth for ten days, found his snoring and sleep got dramatically worse. Mouth breathing, especially at night, is linked to poorer sleep and dental problems. Today: notice how you breathe while working or walking. If your mouth is open, gently close it and breathe through your nose. Try it during light exercise too.
Slow down your breathing

Most of us breathe quickly and shallowly without realising it, especially when stressed. Nestor describes research showing that slowing down to around six breaths a minute, about five seconds in and five seconds out, has a calming effect on the nervous system, heart rate and blood pressure. It's a practice found in many traditions, from yoga to prayer. Today: set a timer for three minutes and breathe in for five seconds, out for five seconds. Notice how your body feels afterwards.
Exhale longer to relax

Breathing out more slowly than you breathe in activates the body's rest-and-digest system, the opposite of fight-or-flight. It's a quick, invisible tool for calming down before a stressful conversation, an exam or bedtime. One simple pattern is to breathe in for four counts and out for six or eight. You can do it anywhere, and no one will notice. Today: before your next stressful moment, take five breaths with a long, slow exhale. Feel your shoulders drop.
Breathe less, not more

It sounds backwards, but Nestor reports that many people breathe more air than they need, and over-breathing can actually reduce how efficiently oxygen reaches our tissues. Several breathing methods train people to breathe lighter, slower and quieter, and athletes sometimes use them to improve endurance. The idea isn't to hold your breath until it hurts, but to stop gulping air. Today: sit quietly for two minutes and try making each breath a little softer and slower than feels natural, without straining.

books.title: The Body Keeps the Score
books.author: Bessel van der Kolk
books.description: A psychiatrist on how trauma lives in the body, and the approaches that help people heal.
ideas: Trauma is stored in the body

Bessel van der Kolk, a psychiatrist who has worked with trauma survivors for decades, argues that trauma isn't only a memory; it lives in the body. After overwhelming experiences, the body's alarm system can stay switched on, showing up as tension, exhaustion, sudden anger or numbness long after the danger has passed. Survivors may feel unsafe in their own skin without knowing why. Understanding this can bring relief: these reactions aren't weakness, they're the body trying to protect itself. Today: notice where you hold tension, your jaw, shoulders or stomach, and breathe gently into that place.
Talking isn't always enough

Because trauma affects parts of the brain that sit below language, talking about it isn't always enough to heal. Van der Kolk describes how approaches that involve the body, such as yoga, movement, breathwork, rhythm, theatre and touch, can help people feel safe and in control again. These methods work alongside talking therapy, not instead of it. Healing often happens through experience, not just understanding. Today: if you carry stress in your body, try ten minutes of gentle stretching or slow movement and notice how you feel afterwards.
Safety comes from connection

One of the strongest protections against the lasting effects of trauma is feeling seen, heard and supported by other people. Van der Kolk notes that we are social creatures and our nervous systems calm down in the presence of people we trust. Isolation makes recovery harder; connection makes it possible. This applies to everyday stress too. Today: reach out to someone you feel safe with, not necessarily to talk about anything difficult, just to share some time together.
Reclaiming the body

Many trauma survivors learn to ignore their bodies, because paying attention to bodily feelings can bring back distress. Van der Kolk explains that healing involves gradually learning to notice sensations, a racing heart, warmth or tension, without being overwhelmed, and to feel at home in yourself again. It's a slow, gentle process, often best done with skilled support. Today: spend one minute noticing the sensations in your hands and feet. Just observe them, with curiosity rather than judgment.
